claims.text: The WiredTiger journal is a write-ahead log used to recover changes after the last checkpoint; journal compression changes the representation of this recovery data. (high confidence)

MongoDB's standalone procedure changes journalCompressor, cleanly shuts down mongod, confirms the process has stopped, and restarts with the new configuration; --wiredTigerJournalCompressor is the command-line alternative. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Use db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.log to monitor journal statistics when evaluating compressor changes. (high confidence)

Mark Callaghan’s March 2014 insert benchmark reported roughly 10% more inserts per second for some configurations with journal compression disabled. The post tested MongoDB 2.6.0-rc0; this is historical evidence, not a measured WiredTiger or current-version improvement. (low confidence)

SERVER-17251 reported an apparent throughput effect from journalCompressor even with journaling disabled on MongoDB 3.0.0-rc8, but MongoDB closed it as Cannot Reproduce; the issue does not establish a confirmed compressor performance regression. (low confidence)

MongoDB's journaling documentation states that WiredTiger does not compress log records of 128 bytes or less, its minimum log-record size; journal-compression savings therefore cannot be assumed for those records. (low confidence)

MongoDB 8.0 documents storage.wiredTiger.engineConfig.journalCompressor with default snappy and supported values none, snappy, zlib, and zstd; Dell's deployment guide shows the same journal-specific configuration. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Journal compression and collection block compression are separate settings: engineConfig.journalCompressor controls journal data, while collectionConfig.blockCompressor controls collection blocks. Treating collection compression results as journal-specific savings would conflate these settings. (high confidence)

WiredTiger does not compress journal records whose size is less than or equal to 128 bytes. The implementation README also describes a small-record exception, but leaves its threshold uncertain. (medium confidence)

Google's Snappy documentation describes a design that favors high speed and reasonable compression over maximum compression. Its compression ratios vary substantially with the input; these algorithm benchmarks are not measurements of MongoDB journal savings. (low confidence)

Inference: for compressible journal records, compression can reduce journal bytes and file turnover relative to none. Actual benefit depends on record size and compressibility, so a fixed journal cost-reduction percentage is unsupported. (medium confidence)
If mongod shuts down uncleanly during a journal-compressor change, MongoDB instructs operators to recover using the old compressor settings before retrying the change. (low confidence)

Journal files are preallocated; WiredTiger removes old files while retaining those needed for recovery from the last checkpoint. Therefore compression ratio alone is insufficient to size the journal directory. (low confidence)

Selecting journalCompressor=none disables compression of journal data. It does not disable journaling: MongoDB's journaling documentation states that journaling is always enabled starting in 6.1 and storage.journal.enabled was removed. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

db.serverStatus() exposes journal statistics in wiredTiger.log. The journaling documentation describes this field as information about the WiredTiger journal; it does not present a universal compression-savings percentage. (medium confidence)

WiredTiger removes journal files no longer needed for recovery from the last checkpoint. MongoDB warns that disabling compression changes journal-space calculations and that insufficient journal disk space can crash the server, so journal compression does not justify eliminating recovery headroom. (low confidence)
